1,	2, 3 and 4. Post office money orders may be purchased on most foreign countries at all accounting post offices in Canada. The procedure in regard to the issuing to the public of post office money orders on foreign countries has not been changed since 1930, with the exception of post office money orders drawn on France. In accordance with the request of the French postal administration, the procedure in regard to the issuing of post office money orders on France was changed as from the 6th May, 1935. obvious that this return and the succeeding 21 returns would, if given effect to, involve the expenditure of large sums of money. It would be impossible to have these returns made during the present session of parliament. Usually information of this kind is obtained from the public accounts committee of the house because the auditor general's report sets out in detail the payments that are made. This is an unusual return to be asked for as it involves considerable toil and the expenditure of large sums of money for something which may not be of much public value. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has considered his motion from the standpoint of the amount of labour and the expenditures involved but if there is any information he would like to have, the various files could be made available, which would represent the minimum of expense and labour. speechtext:
On May 28, on the orders of the day, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) drew my attention to a question asked on January 17 last, relative to the seizure of the schooner "Paul T", and referred particularly to the discrepancy between the official answer to the third part of his question, as tabled in the house on January 24 and appearing on page 157 of Hansard of that day, and the answer which was handed to him by officials of the house. I was absent from the house and was not in Ottawa in the month of January when this question was answered and consequently was not in a position to discuss the matter when my hon. friend referred to it a few days ago.
Seizure of Schooner Paul T.

However, I have now made very careful inquiry and have ascertained that an answer to the hon. member's question was prepared in the department in the usual way. On being reviewed, prior to tabling in the house, it was felt that the answer to the third part of the question might not be considered quite adequate and accordingly a new answer was prepared in the form in which it appears in Hansard. The only reasonable explanation I can offer for the delivery to my hon. friend by officials of the house of the copy of the answer as originally drafted rather than as finally tabled is that in tabling the official answer a copy of the original draft must have been inadvertently attached thereto. In these circumstances I can merely express my regret for the incident and for any inconvenience it may have caused my hon. friend.

subtopic: SEIZURE OP SCHOONER PAUL T.-DISCREPANCY BETW'EEN ANSWER TABLED AND ANSWER HANDED TO MEMBER
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am prepared to accept the explanation of the Minister of National Revenue, because I realize that at that time he was incapacitated through illness and perhaps could not give that attention to the matter which it required. But the explanation as to how the official answer, which after all is the official document, reached my hand, is not satisfactory. Under standing order 44, (2) (b) provides:
If a member does not distinguish his question by an asterisk, the minister to whom the question is addressed hands the answer to the Clerk of the House, who causes it to be printed in the official reports of the debates.
The answer sent to me through one of the pages, after it had been placed on the table, had no attachment whatever to it; it was the simple answer usually given and with the minister's name attached to it. The answer as it appears in Hansard could not have passed through the hands of the officials of this house. If it had. that would have been handed to me. It was not handed to me. The only document that passed through their hands and that was handed to me in answer to the third question contained this reply: "No specific instructions."
The question arises: How did this additional or improved answer, after the department had made the first answer and considered it not sufficiently full, reach Hansard? It is due to the house, as a protection which every member has a right to have, that any answer handed officially to any member should not be other than that which appears in Hansard. I claim as a privilege not only to me but to every hon. member and we have a right to find out how it is that that document got into Hansard in the way it did. It never, I am 
informed, passed over the tables of the house in that shape. It passed over the tables of the house only in the shape in which it was handed to me.
When that answer was handed to me, I considered it very serious, and based upon it, a few days later I made a certain charge in the house. That charge was investigated. I am not going to discuss to-day the process of that investigation; I shall do so at some future date. Had I received the answer that appeared in Hansard which pointed out that the vessel in question had been seized by the provincial government and afterwards handed over to the dominion authorities for action on the part of the preventive service or the Department of National Revenue, I would have hesitated to make the statement I made in the house. When I got the plain and straight answer that no specific instructions had been given for the destruction of the food stores, I felt justified, with the information in my possession, to make the charge I did.
Later on I am brought face to face with what appears in Hansard, an answer that never was given on the floor of the house, and it is demanded of me to prove the charge in the face of the answer that was given in the house as appearing in Hansard, when that answer, I repeat, was never given here. This is not treating an hon. member in an honest, fair and equitable way; when such a thing is allowed to take place, how can we depend upon the truthfulness of Hansard as it appears as an official record of this house? Is it possible to depend upon Hansard in the future if such tactics as those are allowed to take place in the House of Commons? Under those conditions I must protest and I must ask that further information be given to the house as to how that answer got into Hansard instead of the one that was officially given to me across the table.

I really think I ought to be allowed some latitude in this matter as I am the party who has been affected and has suffered on account of it. The Secretary of State says that I should have looked at Han-92582-211
sard on the following day to see what the official reply was. Why should I be called upon to look at Hansard when I have the official answer and have placed it upon my file? That is what I relied upon. May I say also that unrevised Hansard is not accepted in evidence as proof and, as an unrevised edition of Hansard, it is not an official document until after a certain period. I did not look at Hansard; it has not been my habit to scan Hansard every day. Even when I make a speech, I very seldom read it over in Hansard. Perhaps it would have been better for me had I adopted the practice of reading over in Hansard everything I had said or that others had said in which I was interested. By doing so I would perhaps have discovered errors that creep into the reports of things I have said in this house, inadvertently no doubt-by the reporters, which reports I should have looked at myself in order to have corrected. I repeat that I received what was given to me across the table of the house, handed to me in the usual way which has been the practice for years and years. I accepted it, as every hon. member would have done, as the official record of this house, and when the Secretary of State says that he had three copies it is very clear that the only copy that was wrong was the one that was handed to me. I am not attempting to blame him, I do not know who is to blame, but I repeat that an injustice has been done to me personally and to the members of this house in general, and I claim that the matter should in some way be rectified. I do not accept the explanations given here this afternoon as sufficient to justify what was done.

Mr. Chairman, I just
want to say a word to gather up the information which my hon. friend has given with regard to item 451e, slide, hookless or zipper fasteners, on which the duty has been increased ten per cent. My hon. friend gave the number of employees in this industry in 1934 as 115, and the amount of wages paid as $123,815. There were imported into Canada in that year $285,000 worth of these goods, and there were made in Canada $319,000 worth, a total of $604,000. Taking that total amount at twenty per cent, which I think was the rate of duty then, would mean that the people of Canada have paid practically the full wage bill of the industry in increased prices. In other words, whoever the firm or firms are, they have received in increased prices practically the full amount of their wage bill, and by increasing the duty another ten per cent it means that as against a wage bill of $123,000 in 1934 they would receive with the new rate of duty $180,000 in increased prices. The minister may say that I am unfair in that I am including in that figure the amount of goods which were imported. Perhaps I should not say that the amount which the firms receive will be increased by that figure; the amount which would be paid in increased prices by the people of Canada would be $120,000 under the present tariff and $180,000 under the proposed increase, a portion of which would go into the treasury of Canada, but the greater portion of it would go to the firms who are making this commodity. I submit that there should be the strictest inquiry as to the value of the industry to Canada as compared with the amount of taxes which are imposed on

Canadian consumers in order to keep up this industry by means of the increased protection granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one could
discuss at length the question to what extent the statement of my hon. friend is true, that the purchaser or importer pays the duty. If my hon. friend is right in assuming that the duty is in all cases paid by the purchaser or importer, then his statement upon that point would hold good, but as my hon. friend knows, it by no means follows that because the duty is twenty per cent or any other percentage it is paid entirely by the purchaser or importer. My hon. friend no doubt knows, as I do myself, of cases where the importer pays not a cent of the duty, and of other cases where it is divided. But I do not think this is the particular place to debate the point. I only wish to say to my hon. friend and to the committee that whether the decision qua tariff with respect to this item is right or not it is after all based upon the finding of the tariff board after exhaustive inquiry and report, and the basis of their finding, as evidenced by their report, was the relative cost of production of the same commodity in other countries as compared with the cost of production in Canada. Having said so much, in view of the statement which I made before that it has been the policy of the government to implement the findings of the tariff board in all instances, I think nothing further need be said. In other words, we must assume that the tariff board is properly performing its functions, and that being so, I do not want to go behind their findings. Having confidence in the board I propose to pursue in the future the course I have followed in the past of accepting their reports and implementing them by legislation.

When the budget resolutions were before the committee I took advantage of that fact to urge a reduction of the tariff on aeroplanes. Since then I have received a letter from Fairchild Aircraft Limited in which they seem to feel that some of the statements made here were not quite fair to that particular company, and in fairness to the company I should like the privilege of quoting briefly two or three paragraphs from their letter. They say:
We note in the press your remarks made in the House of Commons on May 31, in connection with the tariff as applied to aircraft. We read these with great interest, as it is gratifying ito know that the part which aircraft can play in the development of Canada is being recognized. There are one or two points on which yon have however been misinformed, and we take the liberty of submitting for yonr consideration a brief description of the activities of this company, which is but one unit of the Canadian aircraft industry.
With the exception of engines, we completely manufacture in every detail aircraft designed by our own engineering staff, and we believe the aircraft we produce are better suited to Canadian flying conditions than any obtainable elsewhere.
We have been in continuous operation since 1930 and at the present time employ 135 men. The payrolls for 1934 totalled $81,000 and we expect this figure will be doubled this year.
I asked the minister if he could give us any information with regard to the production of aeroplanes in Canada during the last two years but he did not have the information before him. He has given us the figures for 1933 and I have put part of this letter on Hansard so that this company might know that I did not intend to misinform the house in connection with the development of the industry in Canada. A few days ago I was asked the price quoted by the Bellanca aircraft company for one of their machines. I did not have the information before me but for the benefit of the hon. member who asked the question I should like to quote a paragraph from a letter I received from this company, as follows: Enclosed are specifications for the latest type of Bellanca pacemaker, using a Wright engine. You will note that the horsepower is 420 and

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Power to restore duties which have been reduced on liquors.
Is this the first time an attempt to control prices in the interests of the consumer has been made under the provisions of the customs tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter of dealing with duties by order in council is not new but this phase is new. It is introduced merely for the purpose of ensuring that the object of the reduction in the duty will be fulfilled. Otherwise we would be in the hands of the provincial liquor commissions which might set at naught the reductions made.

Can the minister give us any assurance that the reduction in the excise and the customs duty on liquors will secure the result which he hopes to secure, the stopping of bootlegging? Can he tell U3 that or is it all a matter of guesswork as to just what the result will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am surprised at such a consistent exponent of the doctrice of lower duties and freer trade asking whether a reduction in duty will mean a reduction in the cost of the article. We believe that if the price of liquor is placed at a figure where the ordinary man who desires to purchase feels that he is able to do so, he will prefer to purchase sound liquor from a legitimate source such as a liquor commission rather than to run the risk of buying an unsound

Customs Tariff Amendment
commodity through illicit channels. While I do not believe we have gone far enough, to the extent to which we have gone I think we will contribute to eliminating the illicit sale and purchase of liquors.

I should like to revert to section 3. If this section is invoked for the purpose of reducing duties, is it the intention of the government to bring to parliament for ratification any trade agreement which embodies those reductions in the tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend is aware, if it is a full treaty it comes to parliament as a matter of course, but I believe the practice in the past has been not to bring to parliament those matters which are dealt with by order in council under section 11.

I cannot speak with
authority as to the practice in the past but I submit that it is the constitutional practice to bring to parliament any treaty or agreement which affects statutory provisions. I understand that there is a blanket provision here which permits the reduction of duties but at the same time I have always understood that trade agreements were brought to parliament as a matter of constitutional practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, or treaties.
Ratification is asked for as . a matter of constitutional practice although possibly not as a matter of strict legal necessity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Concessions have been made by order in council which were not brought to parliament for the purposes of ratification, although parliament is entitled to the information. The action taken by order in council by virtue of this section is operative but it is always subject to the overriding action of parliament. Do I understand my hon. friend to suggest that in all cases the action taken should be brought to parliament for ratification?

I am distinguishing constitutional practice from legal necessity. I understand that trade agreements and trade treaties are brought to parliament for ratification as a matter of course notwithstanding the fact that the governor in council might have the power under some blanket authority such as section 11 to conclude an arrangement for the reduction of duties. I want to know if that practice will be followed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend and I are in agreement as to what is the strict
constitutional or legal condition with respect to trade treaties or agreements, and I shall not discuss that matter at the moment. That is the practice which was obtained, that is the practice which should obtain and that is the practice which will be followed. Beyond that there are certain actions taken by order in council which are neither trade agreements nor treaties. In the past these matters have not been brought to parliament for ratification, though parliament should have the information; but I can assure my hon. friend that it is our purpose to adhere strictly to the practice which has obtained hitherto with respect to treaties and trade agreements
Can the minister mention any instance in which it has not been done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For example, we passed to Australia and South Africa under this section by order in council concessions by way of reduction in duty as a result of the operation of the French treaty. That would be a case in point illustrative of what I had in mind when I spoke of action other than by trade treaties or trade agreements.

I do not think that would be under section 11 because under this section the provision is that the governor in council may reduce duties by way of compensation for concessions received from the particular country in whose favour the duties are reduced, and the application of the French treaty provisions to Australia would not bring it within that category.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case there was a specific concession on the part both of South Africa and of Australia.

As regards the amendment made by section 3, whereby the word "concessions" is introduced, has the minister anything particular in mind in that respect? What is the nature of the concessions other than reduction in duties which it is contemplated might permit the governor in council to take action under section 11.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Australia would be a case particularly in point. We could not strictly say in that instance that they had reduced the duty, which would enable us to make a corresponding reduction here, but they gave us a concession by way of margin which was one of real value to us, though strictly speaking it was not a reduction in duty. That is why there is this amendment. It is really, in a sense, widening the spirit of the section- perhaps that is not the correct language. It
Customs Tariff Amendment

is carrying out the intent and purpose of the section, but changing the verbiage to meet the condition I have referred to.

Wfyat I had in mind was whether or not a concession by way of a treaty respecting the St. Lawrence waterways, for instance, would be regarded as a concession under section 11 and so enable the governor in council to reduce tariffs as a quid pro quo.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be a question of fact. I should not care for a moment to attempt to follow the interpretation to its furthest ramifications, but I say in all deference to the committee that it would be a question of fact and of interpretation as to whether it would be a concession coming properly within the spirit and the intent of the section.

I understand from the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and of the reply given by the minister that the governor in council has authority to reduce the tariff, for which we may receive some concession from some other country. My impression is-and this is the point on which I should like to have information-that the governor in council has authority to make reductions whether a concession is received from some other country or not. It might be deemed in the interests of Canada alone to reduce the tariff, without reference to the circumstances affecting other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all right; there is always the sovereign right of this or any other country to take such tariff action as it chooses. Parliament is supreme.
I mean the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am following the argument. Section 11 of the Customs Tariff has specific reference to reciprocal tariff reductions and the wording is:
The governor in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on goods imported into Canada from any other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for reductions on Canadian products granted by any such country or countries.
But they could do it in any event, whether they got a concession or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly; there is always the sovereign right of parliament in the matter. But we are dealing with reciprocal action between two countries, without parliament. That is all that section 11 is for. Here, 
instead of using the words "reductions on Canadian products" we say "concessions"; that is the change.
Is there any objection to making that "tariff concessions" rather than merely "concessions"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know of no immediate objection to the use of those words except that it makes the operation of the section unduly restrictive. There might very well be some other consideration which would be deemed of value to this country and which would warrant making a concession by way of the tariff. I can readily see that a situation of that sort might arise. It might be a question of margin, for example.
But it is a tariff concession.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it is a concession. I do not press the matter at all. I would be content to take the phrasing my hon. friend suggests. I see no objection, if it is a real concession given us by another country, why we should not be able to go beyond the bounds of customs action alone.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to have the matter made clear with respect to what may be pending in the way of negotiations. We were advised the other day by the Prime Minister that negotiations respecting a trade agreement with the United States were still proceeding but might not be concluded before the close of the session. As I understand the minister, if anything in the form of an agreement were entered into between the United States and Canada, following constitutional practice that agreement would have to be submitted to parliament for approval. On the other hand, it is possible that the negotiations proceeding between the two countries might take the form of some reduction of tariffs on each side, in which event the reduction of tariff on one side would be regarded as a compensation or concession for a reduction of tariff on the other. In that case, under the legislation now proposed, the governor in council would have power by order in council to reduce the duties without reference to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Apart from any question of interpretation, I would not have the slightest hesitation in saying to my right hon. friend that in anything so important as a trade agreement with a country such as the United States, it follows as a matter of course that it should be subject to ratification by parliament. That is not the kind of agreement in contemplation which would enable the country to secure con-

Customs Tariff Amendment
cessions by way of order in council under section 11. I want to make that abundantly clear.
Mr. LUCHKOVI'CH: I understand that there is a reduction on liquors. Why has it been limited to liquors? Why should it not be applied to machinery? We in the west like our liquor as well as anybody and would rather get it cheaper than we can at the present time. But we should prefer to have this section made applicable to farmers' machinery, for we certainly need cheap machinery in the west to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not aware that there is any bootlegging in machinery or any illicit importation. If there were it could be dealt with similarly. That was the reason for the action taken. It is not a question of cheapening the product as such; it was a question of attempting in this way to make at least a contribution toward the elimination of bootlegging.

I do not want to delay the committee, but I would ask the minister to consider inserting the word "tariff" before the -word "concessions." It is advisable that we keep tariff matters within the tariff ambit rather than to contemplate some bargain the consideration on one side of which might have nothing whatever to do with tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be pleased to consider the matter. If the committee in its wisdom decides to report the bill, I can hold the third reading and, if it is thought advisable, it can be moved back into committee. There is nothing in my mind other than having an instrument which will be of use; that is all. It may be thought wise on reflection to limit it in the sense suggested by my hon. friend.

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 80, to amend the Income War Tax Act.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Company rate of tax.

I would like to ask one
question on behalf of the municipalities of the province of Ontario. Any section of this bill might serve to cover it. I introduced a resolution on coordination of income tax in this house on this question in 1927, and it was continued in 1928 and 1929. From 1867 down to the introduction of the Income War Tax Act in 1917 the income tax was the exclusive field of' the municipalities. As we all know, at present the municipalities are having a very difficult time owing to conditions. Their sources of revenue are restricted by statute. There has been a gross invasion of their field both by the dominion and by the provinces. I do not object to the dominion levying income tax, because they had to carry on the war, relief and unemployment, and have other heavy burdens. But the present Ontario government have announced that next fall a special session of the legislature is to be convened in order that we shall be given the unexpected joy in the province of Ontario of a triplicate income tax. The income tax of the dominion government is collected chiefly in Ontario and Quebec; a very small part comes from the other provinces. The returns from the city of Toronto for the last year of record were $17,486,000, and for the city of Montreal, $18,893,000. I raised the question of the legality of this provincial tax in 1927, and I think the question is a cogent one whether the proposed tax by the province of Ontario is direct or indirect and the method of collecting illegal. The method of collecting it is both direct and indirect.
This burden of a third income taxation is going to retard the growth of industry in Ontario. There should be some coordination, because in view of the period of unrest we are going through and the condition of business to-day, industry cannot carry any further burdens. I should like to know if any negotiations on this matter have taken place with the provinces, or whether any reference is to be made to the supreme court, because it is in the interest of the taxpayers and the provinces that it should be done. This income tax comes very largely out of the working classes. They had an investigation of this in Washington and it showed a dreadful state of affairs-people like Pierpont Morgan with an income of millions paying no inoome tax at' all. They are now bringing in a provision

Income War Tax Act
for registration, I may say that there is registration to-day in Toronto on municipal income tax and there are facilities there for anyone to go to the city hall office and find what income taxes have been paid. Are we going to wait for the Ontario government to put the cards on the table? As far as the assessment rolls and the collector's rolls are concerned you can walk into the office of the city clerk and turn up the rolls and find out what every person and corporation is paying in income tax to the municipality. The same applies to wills, deeds, and bills of exchange and hen notes and many other matters; they are all registered and open to inspection by the public, and I do not see any reason why there should not be similar publicity concerning income tax
As one of the representatives of an industrial city I protect against a third or provincial income tax in Ontario. The cities are already paying more than they can 'afford for the burden of government. It is all very well to talk about maritime rights and Pacific rights and prairie rights, but what about the rights of the old industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec who pay over 84 per cent of the federal income tax? We hear a lot about the rights of minorities, but what about the rights of majorities who have to pay all these taxes to maintain this country? I protest against this tax by the province. Under section 92 of the British North America Act they have the right of direct taxation to raise revenue for provincial purposes, but not by the widest extension of imagination can it be said that the provinces should take from the municipalities the income tax powers of taxation which they have held from time immemorial. I do not know what is to become of the municipalities of Ontario if they do not get some relief. Are we to wait, year after year, and have these provincial burdens increased? It would be a godsend to the people of this country if there had never been provincial governments. It was the greatest mistake the fathers of confederation ever made; it was done for political rather than for economic reasons, and we see the result in overtaxation and over government.
I have been asked to mention this matter on behalf of some of the municipalities which are being crushed at the present time owing to the burden of relief. A large number of properties are up for sale for arrears of taxes; in many cases the mortgagee has taken possession, and now are we going to add another income tax? This government or any other government in charge of the affairs of this country at present and for years to come will no doubt have to have this federal income tax. The present government and the minister have taken over regarding relief from some municipalities .many of their obligations; in fact I do not know where the municipalities would have been had we not had the Unemployment Relief Act, as the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) mentioned in connection with Montreal, It is not the only city in which that situation exists; almost every large city in the country would have been in an even worse .position than it is at present had it not been for the very active support which the federal government gave to the larger municipalities. But when we have an announcement from the Ontario government that they are going to ask publication of income tax matters and require affidavits or [DOT]provide that people may be examined on oath by the local commissioner, and when you see what they are doing in the United States, allowing people to go to the register and see what is being paid, then I think that in the interest of more revenue for this government a similar amendment might be made in the law here. I do not wish to detain the minister;
I am sorry on his account for having to mention the matter, because I have a great admiration and respect for him and sympathy with him in respect to the burden he has had to bear for the last ten years, not only in this parliament but as a provincial leader. But I should like to hear from him anything he can say in a few words as to the legality of the .proposed provincial tax and the method of collection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think there is
any question as to the right of the provinces to impose this tax. It is a direct tax. As far as it is a direct tax it is strictly within their legislative competence. Neither is there any question as to the right of the dominion to impose this tax. That was settled in the case of the King v. Caron, which went to the privy council, the judgment being delivered by Lord Haldane, who decided that the dominion had jurisdiction. It is perhaps unfortunate that there should be a threefold tax, but as far as that is concerned the question is between provinces and municipalities and is one which must be settled within the province; it is not one which we can settle here. There are certain phases of the incidence of this tax which do work an injustice. That is, a man has a certain income, and income tax is imposed by the dominion. When the province imposes an income tax it is imposed not upon the residue of his income after he has paid the tax to the dominion, but upon his whole income as though he had actually received it, although as a matter of fact he has parted with a portion of it. The
Income War Tax Act

same statement applies to its application in the case of the municipalities. We had that, among other things, in mind when we sought to have a dominion-provincial conference last autumn. The question of income tax was placed upon the agenda of the proposed conference and I think it was unfortunate that we were unable to have that conference, because that was one subject that perhaps we could have dealt with in a manner that would have made it more equitable in its application not only as between the dominion and the provinces but perhaps also as to the individuals whether they pay taxes to the provinces or to the dominion. As a matter of fact, however, we could not have the conference for the reason that we could not secure the attendance of representatives of all the provinces; more than one raised objection to a conference being held at that time. Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do hope, however, that
for the wellbeing of the country the incoming government, whether it be this or another government, will take some action. I notice my hon. friend from Quebec East smiling when I use the term "new government." He has in mind the circumstance that it will be a government of some other party. I had no such circumstance in mind. What I had in mind was that we will have a newly elected government with a newly elected parliament.
I withdraw my smile.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have no misgivings
upon that point; in due course we will know the answer. In all seriousness, however, I do express the hope that there can be a fair and frank discussion between the dominion and provincial governments in the hope that there may result something fairer in the way of the application of income tax. It is all very well to discuss the dominion giving up the tax. Municipalities and provinces are put to it for revenue, but it requires no stretch of the imagination to realize that the dominion government is also in dire need of revenue, and that will be so for a number of years or at all events until some solution has been found of many of the problems we have before us at the present time. So it is idle to discuss giving up this tax, but I do think in fairness we can discuss with the provinces a more equitable application in the hope that it will improve conditions not only as they concern the dominion and the provinces but also as they concern the individual taxpayer.

I am glad to hear what the Minister of Finance has to say with regard to the multiplicity of taxes and the undesirability of such a condition. But I should like to remind him that the government of which he is a member, and in fact the previous government, have practised the same thing even within the dominion itself. I know there is not usually a great deal of consideration or sympathy for corporations or those who derive their incomes from corporations, but if I recite the facts briefly it might be of interest to the committee. So far as income tax is concerned a joint stock company pays on its profits a tax of 13^ per cent. Another business, perhaps of the same nature-and I believe I referred to this last year or two years ago-which happens to be carried on by a partnership or under a single proprietor, making the same amount of profit, escapes that tax altogether. There, I say, is an unjust discrimination. First, so far as the corporation is concerned, there is the 13^ per cent tax. Then when the balance of the profits are distributed among the shareholders they again pay taxes as individuals. Then the provinces come along and exact a tax from the corporation. Now we have the announcement by the premier of the province of Ontario that he is going to propose an income tax also. That will be a fourth tax. Then the municipalities, at least in the province of Ontario, exact still another income tax, so the man who happens to get his income from a joint stock company-and I am no special pleader for those who hold stocks in joint stock companies-is faced with the probability of having to pay five income taxes in one form or another.
I should like to suggest to the minister that he is certainly on the right track when he suggests that there should be some sort of getting together to prevent this multiplicity of taxes. It is perfectly right that those making a great deal of money by way of income from stocks or bonds should pay a proper tax, but surely it cannot be right that the jurisdiction should be spread over municipalities, provinces and the dominion so as to bring about practically fivefold taxation on the same income.
In conclusion I just want to repeat what I said two years ago, or perhaps it was last year, with regard to the absolute injustice of the double taxation now exacted by this government from those who happen to get their incomes from stocks. It is a discrimination against joint stock companies, and after all that is a fair method of doing business. Consider two businesses side by side, perhaps in exactly the same line of business. One is

Income War Tax Act
operated as a joint stock company, perhaps with almost all the stock owned by the same man or the same family. Next to that business or across the street is a firm doing business under a single proprietor or a partnership. The joint stock company pays an income tax of 13J per cent while the other business escapes that tax altogether. In addition all the individuals concerned pay taxation on their incomes. I say this is a double tax that is utterly inexcusable unless it arises through the necessity of securing revenue, and even that ought to be subject to the ordinary laws of fairness and equity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Having said that I do not for a moment want to go back on what I have already stated as to the injustice of the principle of double taxation. It is unjust, and I hope
the time is not far distant when we may be able to get away from it. Before the section is carried I should like to make an observation which I think is in order at this time. There has been much confusion in the minds of many taxpayers this year-probably it existed in previous years also-with regard to the retroactive feature of the changes and increases in the income tax, especially with regard to unearned or investment income. Quite a number of my constituents came to me to find out whether in the returns to be filed April 30 they had to provide for the changes in regard to investment incomes. I directed them to the officers of the Department of National Revenue. I was quite aware, of course, that these changes were retroactive and, consequently, should be provided for in the returns, but the confusion was brought about by the fact that in the first place the changes had not been adopted by the house-in fact they have not been adopted yet-and in the second place the forms supplied to the public made no provision at all for investment incomes. I feel sure therefore, that a large number of the returns that have been received by the department up to the present have made no provision at all for that new feature. I will take the stand that perhaps it might be a good thing for this government or the government to come to consider the advisability of not making these changes retroactive. I understand that it has been working both ways When the income tax was reduced by the former government it did apply to the previous year, and therefore when it is increased it seems only fair that it should be made retroactive, but there may come a time when the income tax will be increased by such an amount that the income tax payer will not have made any provision to meet the increased tax exacted from him, and I am not sure that it would not be advisable to consider whether, when changes are made in the income tax, the new tax should be made applicable to the current and not to the previous year. However, that was not my point.
I am quite aware that a large number of taxpayers have probably not provided for the investment income in their returns this year.

So I can speak feelingly of the position the taxpayer finds himself in who is called upon to pay a heavier tax in a year when his income has been greatly reduced. It is very difficult to defend that, but before we can alter our system we have to have a treasury overflowing to such an extent that we can forego one year's income tax. As I have pointed out most of the changes were downward rather than upward, and I submit that regardless of who does it, it is wrong, it is unjust, it is unfair, it is inequitable, it is not good legislation to make increases in taxation or changes in the law apply to a period that has already been closed, the commitments for which have already been undertaken, the disbursements for which have already been made. As I suggested in the discussion on the resolution, it seems to me to involve a violation of what is an implied contract between the government and the taxpayer that his taxes for that period will be so much. on the full indemnity notwithstanding that the member in Ottawa has to spend a certain amount of money to earn that indemnity. It seems proper that an allowance should be made-the country would not criticize it in the slightest-to members of parliament who actually spend money for living expenses in Ottawa to become entitled to the indemnity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I accede to the view expressed by my hon. friend. As a matter of fact an indemnity is not an income at all, otherwise it is not an indemnity. 1 can speak with some knowledge going back more particularly to the years when 1 was first in the house, when we received $2,500. I never took a cent back to my constituency, and the demands upon the member at that time were as heavy as they are to-day and as numerous. I will go further. I think the question of living expenses in Ottawa ought to be taken into consideration. It is grossly unjust to regard the indemnity of members as income for purposes of income tax, and I commend to the incoming parliament-
Why not now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would have done it willingly myself but for the fact that my motives would have been misconstrued.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The new parliament is the body to take action of that kind, and so far as I am concerned, wherever I may be, I will subscribe to it fully. I do not hesitate to say frankly that I believe the Income Tax Act should be amended to exempt the indemnities of senators and members of parliament, because if they are not income they are not subject to taxation. Indemnities are what the name implies: they are merely intended to indemnify members for the sacrifice they make in expenditure and in time and in giving up their income to come to Ottawa. I make that statement with the greatest satisfaction, and I do hope that the new parliament will be much wiser and kinder to its members than this parliament and the preceding ones have been.

The minister will find
in the Department of Justice an opinion of Sir Allen Aylesworth, a distinguished lawyer, who in strong language claims that this imposition of a tax on the indemnities of members and of senators is ultra vires the powers of this parliament and is unconstitutional.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Whether it is or not, I
have no hesitation in saying that it is unjust. I do not think it should be continued.

I would direct the attention of the minister to expenses which we are allowed to deduct in determining our net income. For the last five years there has been a distinct difference of opinion between myself and the inspector as to whether or not I should receive an allowance at all for the fact that I require the use of an automobile. I use it both in my business, in carrying on my farm, and in earning my indemnity. I have a large constituency and I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that in carrying out my duty as I am expected by my constituents to do it, I must cover at least 5,000 or 6,000 miles of country roads every year. In addition to that, I do a good deal of travelling back and forth to my farm. I am using my car in carrying on my farming operations part of the time and on other occasions I am using it in earning my indemnity. I have been consistently opposed in that view by the inspector of income tax. I really think that right and justice would be on the side of any man in my position, that is in using a car either in the superintending of his farming operations or in earning his indemnity in visiting his constituents. As I have been unable to get any redress through the inspector of income tax, I want to give the matter a little publicity while we have the minister and the commissioner of income tax here. I think I am justly and legally entitled to an allowance for the use of my car, because men in almost every other occupation are getting an allowance for that; they are being allowed to deduct the expenses incurred in running their cars, and certainly a similar allowance in this connection should be made to members.

I would like to endorse the
remarks of the last speaker. It is well known we incur expenses solely and entirely in connection with being members of parliament, and yet we are not allowed to deduct as part of our expenses, for instance, the hire of stenographic help and payment of travelling expenses. Like my hon. friend, I have endeavoured to charge this up and have not been allowed to do so. I understand some yeare ago an amendment was inserted in the act which allowed a commercial traveller when he was away from home, to make a charge for his expenses thus incurred. At that time it was expected' that members of parliament would qualify under that section for exemption, but some wiseacres in the customs or excise decided that being a member of parliament is not an occupation or a busi-

Income War Tax Act
ness-they did not define what it was; a recreation, I presume-and' on that ground the application failed.
I just want to make this suggestion in regard to the remarks of the Minister of Finance; he says that he thoroughly appreciates the situation and he himself would be glad to make the reform that is asked for, but for the fact that it would look as if he were legislating for himself or as if we were legislating for ourselves, and he commended! the reform to the next parliament. But I suggest that now is the correct and precise moment for him to take action and to have it not take effect until the following parliament. That would relieve him and us of the suggestion that we were legislating for ourselves. If it takes effect then, heaven knows who will be here to constitute the next parliament. It is the custom, when any increase in salary for the members of a legislative body is being made, for the outgoing legislature to take the action, because that takes away the reflection of men legislating for themselves. The Minister of Finance evidently has the support of the house in this reform; he is in favour of it; why not pass it now with the condition that it shall not take effect until the next parliament?
Mr. RHODES; I shall be pleased to consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), but I would have to confer with my colleagues before I could take any action. My suggestion, if it is agreeable to the committee, is that we pass this bill, and if my colleagues concur in the idea, which appeals to me personally, I would ask that an amendment be made to the bill in the upper house. So far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to support the idea, but my hon. friend will understand that I cannot take action without conferring with my colleagues.
There is a precedent for this. In British Columbia such a deduction is allowed by the provincial income tax department. It used to be $2,000; now they have reduced it to $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is because it is a matter of law, and that is the difficulty the commissioner of income tax has at the moment with respect to the situation referred to by the hon. member for Macleod in regard to the use of an automobile. The deductions for travelling expenses are laid down specifically in paragraph (f) of section 5 of the Income War Tax Act, which reads: 92582-2124
Travelling expenses, including the entire amount expended for meals and lodging, while away from home in the pursuit of a trade or business.
It is obvious that it would be hard to construe that language to cover a member of parliament as pursuing a trade or conducting a business.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is the noblest of all callings.
If a man has a business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If a member of parliament
has a business which he conducts, that is quite another matter, but my hon. friend was referring to the circumstance that as a member of parliament he requires the use of a motor car in going about and doing government business, and that there should be a deduction on this account. May I say this: If we do have the law amended deleting the indemnity from being taken into account in the income tax, we shall have gone a reasonable distance. I think under those circumstances a member cannot keep a proper check in respect to the use of a motor car on government business.

My complaint was chiefly in regard to the fact that no allowance is made for my expenses in travelling to my farm and back. That certainly was my business as distinct from being a member of parliament and the indemnity one receives therefor. The reply was: If you used this car exclusively for that purpose, the allowance would be made. But as I used it for other purposes I could not seem to convince the inspector of income tax that I should get any allowance for that. I just felt that the act was not being administered fairly in that regard.

May I call the attention of the minister to section 6 (a) of the act which I presume he has 'before him. This gives him additional latitude. It provides that:
In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of

(a) disbursements or expenses not wholly-
This is where they get the hon. member for Macleod, I presume:
-exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the
income.
There the words "trade or business" are not used, and "income" is defined by the statute as including indemnity. I have felt indirectly that can mean that an allowance
Income War Tax Act

could be made where the disbursements were made wholly for the purpose of earning the indemnity; that is to say, expenses for living in Ottawa which are made for no other purpose than earning the sessional indemnity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would be true no
doubt, if the condition continued to obtain that the indemnity was regarded as income.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 4 agreed to.
On section 5-Alternative exemptions from surtax.

I would like to submit
to the minister that in the explanation given of paragraph (c) of clause S there are enumerated the relatives for whom an exemption is allowed. I would point out that this is interpreted very strictly, held to blood relatives. There are men who probably have under their own roofs people whom they are keeping and for whom they can get no allowance. Take the case of a man supporting his foster parents, his stepmother or stepfather. There seems to be an injustice in some cases such as these.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That matter has been up
in the house and discussed and considered many times. In an act of this kind, while it is true that if you do not widen the exemptions, you will do an injustice in an individual case, on the other hand, having regard to the necessity of protecting the revenue, the less opportunity one gives to the taxpayer to evade the tax by enlarging his exemption, the better. For my part I can see no good reason why we should go farther than we have gone at present.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6-Expenses payable to controlling company abroad.

I want to ask a question
on subsection (j). Section 6 as a whole, as I understand, provides that certain items enumerated there are not to be allowed as deductions from net income. Paragraph (j) refers to net losses sustained in the 1934 or any subsequent taxation period in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, et cetera. But I note that insurance companies other than life are exempt from that liability. Would the minister tell us why that exemption is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The answer is that insurance companies doing a world wide business are subject to conditions which do not obtain

in ordinary business, for example conflagration loss. That is the reason that this exemption appears.

In respect to clause (k)
I spoke to one of the officers of the department; is there an amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I am quite prepared
to move an amendment conforming to the suggestion made by my hon. friend, which amendment does not change the section as it was intended to be applied, but would make it clear 'beyond question that it bears that interpretation. I therefore move:
That paragraph (k) of section 6 of Bill 80 be amended by inserting after the word "issued" in the eleventh line, the words "or the income provisions thereof have been adopted" and by inserting after the word "corporation" in the eighteenth line of the said paragraph, the words "or its predecessor."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 7 and 8 agreed to.
On section 9-payments in respect of certain copyrights and copyrighted works.

Does the minister expect to get any increased revenue out of the change? I understand that under this section a uniform rate of five per cent is imposed instead of twelve and a half per cent which was contingent on returns being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, we do not expect any increase.
Or any decrease?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not expect there will be any change.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-Proviso against evasion.

Will the minister consider my remarks in regard to the retroactive provisions of this act applicable to this section? I have not any particular company in mind, so I can speak very freely. What is being done here is to provide that dividends payable to a non-resident company shall be taxable if that company has been incorporated since April 1,
1933.	What appears to have been done, as would appear from the note, is that Canadian companies have been paying dividends to parent companies outside. The practice has grown up of establishing parent companies outside in order that these dividends might be received by them free of tax. It was per-

Income War Tax Act
fectly legal and proper; there was no statutory provision or legal objection to it. Then suddenly this bill comes in to say that if the company was incorporated since April 1, 1933, that remittance from the Canadian company to the parent company is to be taxable. It is simply the retroactive feature over again, which I submit is unfair in principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section was designed purely for the purpose of preventing evasion, not for the purpose of imposing any injustice or any new taxation. It is to prevent the incorporation of a company in order to permit escape from taxes.
It is all right to prevent evasion from this time on, but this is what judicial decisions call avoidance, not evasion. It is perfectly proper to avoid taxation but not to evade it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-Payments on income bonds or income debentures.

This is a section which goes along with subsection (k) of section 6. One of the provisions of section 6 was that interest on income bonds was not to be deducted as an expense of the company. The circumstances under which income bonds are usually issued, as the minister knows, are these; a bondholder has a bond bearing a fixed rate of interest. The company gets into difficulty, and he is approached and told: "If you do not give up your bond, forego your rights and take something less, the company is going into liquidation." The bondholder agrees to some scheme of reorganization under which instead of getting a fixed rate. of interest he gets an income bond, the interest on which is payable only if earned. The bondholder gives up something, makes a contribution in order that a Canadian company may continue operations instead of going into bankruptcy. The minister has inserted in subsection (k) of section 6 a proviso that if income bonds are created under those conditions, under a reorganization in respect of which relief has been given to the debtor corporation, then the interest payable on that income bond is a proper deduction to be made by the company from its operating expenses. I submit that the same principle should apply to section 11, which as it is drawn provides that:
. .. any annual amount received' in respect of an income bond or income debenture shall be deemed to be a dividend.
In other words the bondholder who had his right under his fixed interest bond was getting bond interest, not a dividend, but
having agreed to take something else from the company he now finds it converted into a dividend, which makes it subject to a five per cent deduction under section 9B; so the bondholder is being penalized for having been accommodating and having given up his rights against the company and accepted something less. Therefore I want to ask the minister- I feel sure that he will agree in principle- if he will agree that a man who has consented to a reorganization under the circumstances stated in subsection (k), that is a forced reorganization brought about by financial difficulties, and who has agreed not to exact his pound of flesh, will be treated at least as generously as far as taxation is concerned as he would be if he had retained his rights under his fixed interest bond. That could be done if the minister would insert the proviso of subsection (k) as a proviso of section 11. Although the minister may agree to carry out the idea by way of administration, I think it would be better for certainty if the minister would insert the proviso of subsection (k) in section 11.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I prefer not to make an
amendment, because it would provide an exemption for all time for non-residents. But I will say that it is the intention that this section 11 shall be administered in precisely the same way as the preceding section 6, in a bona fide case such as has been instanced by my hon. friend.

That is the only kind
for which it is asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is quite competent, and
it has been quite competent, to deal with the matter by way of exemption by order in council. Having regard to the danger there would be in widening the provision I think perhaps that is the better method of dealing with it.

Then the minister would
give that assurance, that the principle of subsection (k) will be applied by order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly. The desire
would be to see any bona fide cases, such as the one instanced by my hon. friend, fully protected.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-Exemption from 121 per cent deduction.

Is that subsection (e)
lettered correctly? If the minister will just check it up, I cannot find any subsection (e) in the act or the amendment?

Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is properly included
here, because it has reference to an amendment made last year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 13 agreed to.
On section 14-Tax on gifts.

With regard to subsection
8, paragraph (a), which reads:
... gifts or donations made by any individual the aggregate value of which in any year does not exceed four thousand dollars;
I should like to appeal to the minister to raise that exemption somewhat. It seems to me that gifts somewhat in excess of $4,000 really should be exempt. I have in mind the case of a man who feels that he would like to give the home in which he is living to his wife; I think in many cases there is ample justification for such an act. In many instances he would be compelled to pay a tax on a gift of that kind, because often the home would be valued at more than $4,000. The rate of taxation increases progressively with the size of the gift until the sum of $1,000,000 is reached and it does seem to me that the exemption .might be raised higher than $4,000. It may be that I am taking the wTrong view, because I have not been informed as to the particulars of the gift tax in any other, country where it has been imposed. I presume the minister has made some study of this matter as it works in other countries. Could he tell us whether, in any other country where the tax is in operation, the exemption stops at $4,000? My whole point is that the tax is imposed at too low a point, and that the exemption should be more than $4,000. I believe in many cases this might be regarded as something of a hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we did make inquiry with respect to this tax, which is in operation in other countries. The nearest example is to be found in the United States. The object of the tax is obvious; it is to prevent an individual with an income which would bear a very heavy income tax from escaping that tax by handing over to certain relatives, perhaps to his immediate family, a physical volume of securities, for instance, which would have the effect of dividing his income among five or six persons. These, paying individual income tax, would come under a lower bracket, being in receipt of a smaller income, and in the aggregate the income tax payable by these individuals would

be nothing like the income tax that would be paid by the man under the higher bracket. It was to prevent that sort of thing, without the state securing some compensation by way of revenue, that this gift tax was imposed. The figure originally mentioned in the resolution was $1,000. That was raised, because we did not want to include in the category of gifts which were intended to be taxed, for the reasons I have just indicated, certain bona fide gifts by individuals to members of their families by way of an annual income, for example. There were certain cases of that. Inasmuch as the individual who gives, we will say, an annuity of $4,000 to a member of his family has paid an income tax upon that, the exchequer is not cheated. Possibly $5,000 might be a fairer figure; that is the figure set in the United States. I should be quite content to have it raised to $5,000, but I doubt if we would be wise in increasing the exemption beyond that figure. In that regard I am entirely in the judgment of the committee.
I was under the impression that the bill contained the figure of $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The resolution did mention that amount., but we have made it $4,000 in the bill.

So far as I am concerned I can see why gifts of this size should not be allowed every year, but the gifts I had in mind were those made once or twice in a man's lifetime. He may never have made any gift of the kind before that would assist him in any way by reducing his income tax. I do not want to labour the point, but it did seem to me that the exemption might very well be raised to the point mentioned by the minister, $5,000 or $6 000. However, I am willing to accept the minister's judgment if he thinks $4,000 is the proper amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is fair.
In certain cases it is liable to be regarded as a hardship.
